Physical actions by autonomous devices increasingly require access control decisions based on the surrounding physical context.
Robots and embodied agents are becoming more capable of operating alongside humans, handling objects, accessing infrastructure, and interacting with other autonomous devices without continuous human supervision.
These physical actions can cause real harm to people, objects, and infrastructure when performed under unsafe conditions.
Thus, before allowing a physical action, the the system must verify that the required physical conditions hold.

A delivery robot accessing a networked storage locker illustrates why physical context matters.
Suppose the robot is authenticated and has permission to retrieve an item from the locker.
The locker should nevertheless verify that the robot is physically present before opening, and it may need to ensure that the area around its door is clear.
Similarly, the robot may need to verify conditions around the locker or the item before retrieving it.
Each physical action therefore requires verification of the relevant physical conditions at the time of action.

However, using physical context for access control raises three practical challenges.

\section{Motivation}
\label{sec:motivation}

\subsection{Motivating Scenario}

An authorized operation can still require physical checks before its actions can proceed.
Consider a delivery robot retrieving an item from a networked locker, as illustrated in \figurename~\ref{fig:motivation}.
The robot and locker authenticate each other, and the robot has permission to retrieve the item.
These checks establish who is participating and whether the requested operation is permitted, but they do not establish that the physical conditions required for opening the locker and retrieving the item are met.

The robot and locker must each check the conditions relevant to the action they control.
Before opening its door, the locker must verify that the authenticated robot is in the pickup zone and that the doorway is clear.
Before extending its gripper, the robot must verify that the authenticated locker is within its retrieval zone.
The locker being ready to open does not imply that the robot is ready to retrieve the item, and the robot's presence does not imply that the doorway is clear.
Permission to carry out the operation therefore needs to be combined with physical checks for each action.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \fbox{\parbox[c][1.55in][c]{0.94\columnwidth}{
        \centering
        \textbf{Motivating example placeholder}\\[0.5em]
        Delivery robot and networked locker.\\
        Show proximity verification between the robot and locker,\\
        doorway-clear verification at the locker, and\\
        local physical-context verification at the robot.
    }}
    \caption{Physical-context access control for a delivery robot and networked locker. Although the robot has permission to retrieve the item, each physical action depends on conditions observed at the time of action.}
    \label{fig:motivation}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Why Authentication Is Not Enough}

Authentication identifies a peer but does not establish its presence at the point of physical interaction.
An authenticated robot may communicate with the locker while remaining outside the pickup zone.
A relay can also forward messages between the locker and a remote robot without invalidating the robot's cryptographic responses.
Conversely, detecting an object in front of the locker does not establish that it is the robot identified by the authenticated session.
The presence check must therefore connect physical evidence from the required region to the authenticated peer.

Other physical requirements concern the surrounding environment and can be checked without the peer's participation.
For example, the locker can use its own sensors to check whether its doorway is clear, independently of the robot's identity.
This observation cannot replace the robot-presence check, just as a successful exchange with the robot cannot establish doorway clearance.
The same action can thus require both evidence obtained through a physical exchange with a peer and observations obtained locally.

Physical evidence can become outdated between observation and action.
The robot may leave the pickup zone after its presence has been verified, or an object may enter a doorway that was previously clear.
This matters even within one operation: a result obtained early may become too old while another check is still running.
Each condition therefore needs a limit on how long its verification result may be used, and the endpoint must check those limits immediately before acting.
Such limits constrain the use of old evidence without guaranteeing that a condition remains unchanged until actuation.

These requirements motivate a common way to specify physical checks and carry them out using the resources available at the participating endpoints.
The policy should identify the conditions required for each action, while the system selects suitable verification mechanisms and checks their results before the action proceeds.
Because endpoints may have different sensors and communication hardware, the same policy condition may need different mechanisms across deployments, provided that each mechanism can establish the required condition under the deployment's assumptions.
This separates the physical conditions an application requires from the procedures used to check them.

\section{Background and Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

In this section, we review the authentication, access-control, and physical-verification approaches that inform our design.

\subsection{Authentication and Session Establishment}

Authentication and session establishment provide the cryptographic basis for identifying the participants in a physical exchange.
The Secure Swarm Toolkit (SST) provides authorization services and key management for heterogeneous IoT endpoints~\cite{kim2017toolkit}.
Its authorization service checks communication policies and distributes session keys, which endpoints use to establish secure peer connections.
This infrastructure lets applications obtain authenticated communication without implementing key management themselves.

Our design uses an authenticated peer session to associate subsequent physical evidence with the participating endpoint.
The shared cryptographic context supports responses tied to the peer and the current verification exchange, while the physical mechanism determines what those responses establish about the peer's presence.
Authentication and key establishment are underlying services in the design; Section~\ref{sec:implementation} describes our integration with SST.

\subsection{Context-Aware Access Control}

Attribute-based access control can express conditions involving an entity's environment as well as its identity and permissions.
The NIST ABAC model evaluates attributes of subjects, objects, requested operations, and environmental conditions against access-control policies~\cite{hu2013guide}.
A physical condition, such as doorway clearance, can therefore be represented as an input to policy evaluation.
The remaining question for our setting is how to obtain evidence for that condition and determine whether it is still usable when the action begins.

Policy architectures separate the evaluation of access rules from their enforcement at the protected resource.
XACML distinguishes a policy decision point (PDP), a policy enforcement point (PEP), and policy information points that supply attribute values~\cite{oasis2013xacml}.
It also supports obligations returned with a decision that the PEP must fulfill as part of enforcement.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) similarly evaluates policies over supplied structured data and separates policy decisions from application enforcement~\cite{opaDocumentation}.
OPA can run as a sidecar alongside an application in Kubernetes, placing the policy engine close to the enforcement point~\cite{opaKubernetes}.

Our proposed framework specializes this policy-and-enforcement structure for requirements that need physical evidence before actuation.
The authorization service selects verification mechanisms according to the required conditions and available resources.
The endpoint obtains the evidence, checks the provisioned requirements and freshness bounds, and controls whether its action proceeds.
The contribution concerns this connection between policy requirements, physical evidence acquisition, and action execution; environmental attributes and local enforcement are established parts of access-control architectures.

\subsection{Physical Presence and Proximity Verification}

Physical communication channels can connect a cryptographic identity to a device involved in a local interaction.
Balfanz et al. use location-limited channels to exchange pre-authentication information, such as commitments to public keys, before establishing a secure wireless connection~\cite{balfanz2002talking}.
Their approach relies on physical properties that support identifying the intended devices and detecting unwanted participation.
Our cooperative verification starts with an established authenticated session and uses a subsequent physical exchange to check a requirement for the pending action.

Contextual co-presence techniques infer whether devices share an environment by comparing their observations.
Truong et al. evaluate Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and audio for strengthening zero-interaction authentication, including the effects of combining modalities and manipulating sensed context~\cite{truong2014copresence}.
DoubleEcho uses an emitted acoustic chirp and observations of the room's impulse response to mitigate context-manipulation attacks~\cite{truong2019doubleecho}.
These approaches motivate treating the observation process and its attack assumptions as part of a mechanism's presence claim.

Distance-bounding protocols use the timing of cryptographic challenge--response exchanges to establish an upper bound on a prover's distance.
Hancke and Kuhn prepare responses using a shared secret and then perform a rapid exchange of individual challenge and response bits~\cite{hancke2005rfid}.
The resulting guarantee depends on the timing properties of the physical channel and implementation; attacks exploiting modulation and decoding delays demonstrate why these details matter~\cite{hancke2008attacks}.
Our IR exchange draws on this challenge--response structure, with its acceptance rule and the scope of its presence claim described in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-ir}.

Bluetooth methods estimate proximity and distance, but their security claims depend on the measurement method and adversarial assumptions.
Studies of BLE fingerprinting and ranging characterize the effects of deployment conditions on RSSI and compare it with time-of-flight measurements~\cite{faragher2015location,giovanelli2018rssi}.
Bluetooth Channel Sounding combines phase-based ranging and round-trip timing with dedicated security features~\cite{woolley2024channelsounding}.
However, demonstrated analog relay attacks against Bluetooth access control and distance manipulation in phase-based ranging show that authentication and nominal ranging accuracy alone do not establish relay resistance~\cite{staat2022analog}.
Our mechanism evaluates RSSI from the authenticated peer's active connection as a proximity indicator, with its limitations specified in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-bluetooth}.

Wi-Fi measurements support ranging and localization across indoor and urban deployments.
RADAR and Horus use received signal strength for indoor positioning~\cite{bahl2000radar,youssef2005horus}, while SpotFi and Chronos exploit angle-of-arrival and time-of-flight information for finer spatial estimates~\cite{kotaru2015spotfi,vasisht2016decimeter}.
These observations enable applications including indoor tracking and access-point positioning using mobile measurements and urban information~\cite{bahl2000radar,youssef2005horus,choi2024enhanced}.
Using such estimates for action authorization additionally requires associating the measurements with the authenticated peer and assessing their validity under the deployment's environmental and adversarial assumptions.
Our Wi-Fi mechanism uses RSSI as a calibrated proximity indicator, as described in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-wifi}.

UWB time-of-flight ranging supports precise distance estimation through wideband arrival-time measurements, with accuracy dependent on calibration and propagation conditions~\cite{ieee2020uwb,jimenez2017comparing}.
Compared with RSSI-based proximity estimates, timed exchanges impose stronger constraints on conventional relays because forwarding adds propagation and processing delay.
UWB-PR and analyses of IEEE 802.15.4z scrambled timestamp sequences (STS) examine how waveform and receiver design can support secure ranging~\cite{singh2019uwb,luo2024secure}.
However, security analyses and practical attacks such as Ghost Peak show that cryptographic protection alone does not prevent distance shortening in deployed HRP UWB systems~\cite{singh2021security,leu2022ghost}.
Our framework uses UWB for quantitative proximity checks, with the verification procedure and scope of its guarantee described in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-uwb}.

Our framework connects physical verification mechanisms to the conditions required for individual endpoint actions.
A co-presence result or distance bound is useful only when it establishes the spatial condition required by the policy under the deployment's assumptions.
The framework combines such cooperative checks with local observations, selects mechanisms supported by the participating resources, and checks evidence freshness before actuation.
Section~\ref{sec:mechanisms} examines cooperative co-presence verification using inexpensive physical-channel components within this broader design.

\section{System Overview and Formulation}
\label{sec:formulation}

%% physical requirement specify.
% these requirements

In this section, we first present the system architecture and workflow, then define the system model, threat assumptions, physical requirements, and verification model.

\subsection{System Overview}
\label{sec:approach-overview}

Our design integrates centralized verification planning with endpoint side physical-context checks and action authorization, as illustrated in \figurename~\ref{fig:overview}.
The authorization service uses policy, identity, and resource information to provision an executable plan.
When endpoints need to perform a handshake, the service also selects the communication mechanism they use for that handshake.
Endpoints establish an authenticated session over the selected mechanism when cooperation is required, execute their plans, and check the results immediately before actuation.
The plan may include both local sensor observations and cooperative physical exchanges.
The endpoint makes the physical-action decision locally without a further authorization service round trip.

    \includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/overview.pdf}
    \caption{TODO: The authorization service provisions how physical requirements are verified, while each endpoint evaluates the evidence and authorizes the actions it controls.}
    \label{fig:overview}
\end{figure}

Each endpoint independently decides whether to perform its own action based on the verification results for that action's physical requirements.
An endpoint can deny its action even if the peer's checks succeed.
When an action requires no participation from another endpoint, verification proceeds locally after the endpoint receives its authorization and plan.

\subsection{System Model}
\label{sec:system-model}

%physical endpoint 계속 사용.
%figure로 endpoint.
% sensing and actuation endpoint....
% table: 로 개념들 쭉. term. def. example..
% operation 하나에 action이 여러개 들어간다. set이 아니라 sequence다. ordered set..
% cooperative - individual

Our system comprises physical endpoints that control their own actions and a trusted \textit{authorization service} that specifies the required physical checks.
Endpoints interact with people, objects, and other endpoints, using sensing and communication resources to observe their environment and exchange physical signals with peers.
The authorization service evaluates operation requests using device identities, permissions, and resource information, and prepares verification plans according to policy.
Endpoints execute these plans and decide locally whether to perform the actions they control.

An operation consists of one or more endpoint-controlled actions, each subject to its own physical requirements.
For example, retrieving an item from a locker involves the locker's $\mathsf{OPEN}$ action and the robot's $\mathsf{RETRIEVE}$ action.
The locker may require the robot to be present and the doorway to be clear, while the robot may require an acceptable item temperature.
Each endpoint must satisfy the requirements for its own action, so permission to participate in the operation does not automatically authorize all actions involved.
An operation performed by a single endpoint follows the same model without requiring a peer.

We refer to the process of checking an action's required physical conditions as \emph{physical-context verification}.
Local verification uses the action owner's sensors without requiring another endpoint to participate, while cooperative verification obtains evidence through a physical exchange with a peer.
An action may require both forms, such as local verification of doorway clearance and cooperative verification of peer presence.
For cooperative verification, we assume that the participating endpoints have already authenticated each other and established a shared cryptographic context, allowing the physical exchange to be bound to the peer and session.
An underlying authentication and key-establishment system provides this context and may operate independently of the authorization service.

%% The system can. too long subject. communication channel.
%% The two. 이상함.
% mechanism도 이상함. 
The channel used to establish the authenticated session and the mechanism used to verify physical context are selected independently.
The former carries the authentication exchange, while the latter obtains the physical evidence required by the policy.
The two may use the same hardware, but completing the authentication exchange does not by itself satisfy the physical requirements.


\subsection{Threat Model and Assumptions}
\label{sec:threat-model}

%prevent an endpoint from unauthorized actions.
% 내가 자신을 authorize 한다기 보다는, action을 할지말지를 결정.
% authorization을 endpoint가 하는건 아님. decision point는 auth. 
%pdp pep. 확실히 구분. 
% 그래서 endpoint가 authorize하는게 말이 안된다.
% threat model에 그림...


Our security objective is to prevent an endpoint from authorizing a protected action using physical evidence that is forged, unavailable, or too old for the policy.
We trust the authorization service and the policy, identity, and resource information on which it relies.
At the endpoint controlling the protected action, we trust the verification runtime, local sensor interfaces, clock, and actuator-enforcement path.
We exclude compromise of this endpoint that allows an attacker to bypass verification and directly operate its actuator.
We assume that the underlying authentication and cryptographic mechanisms protect endpoint identities, session integrity, and secret keys.
We exclude collusion in which the peer being verified shares its secret keys with a malicious proxy.

The attacker can interfere with both network communication and the physical signals used for verification.
On the network, the attacker may observe, modify, inject, replay, delay, or relay messages, subject to the cryptographic assumptions stated above.
The attacker may also manipulate or relay physical signals between endpoints.
A relay can forward valid responses from an authenticated peer even when that peer is outside the required physical region.
Resistance to relay attacks depends on each verification mechanism’s assumptions and acceptance criteria; we do not claim protection against all possible relays.
Section~\ref{sec:mechanisms} specifies these physical assumptions for the cooperative co-presence mechanisms considered in this paper.

\subsection{Physical Context Requirements}
\label{sec:requirements}

A \emph{physical requirement} specifies both a condition that must hold before an action and the maximum permitted time between verifying that condition and starting the action.
We represent each requirement as
\begin{equation}
r_i=(p_i,\tau_i),
\end{equation}
where $p_i$ is a predicate over the physical world and $\tau_i$ bounds the delay between its successful verification and the start of the action.
This representation specifies what must be established and how recent its verification must be.

An endpoint may perform an action only when all physical requirements assigned to that action are satisfied.
For endpoint $d$ and action $a$, the policy defines the requirement set
\begin{equation}
R(d,a)=\{r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n\}.
\end{equation}
Each requirement is satisfied only if its predicate passes verification and the verification result meets its freshness bound when the action begins.

A single action can require several physical conditions with different freshness bounds.
For example, opening a locker may require an authenticated robot to be present in the pickup zone and the doorway to be clear.
Let $Z_{\mathrm{pickup}}$ denote the region in front of the locker where the robot must be present to receive an item.
The requirements are
\begin{align}
r_1 &= (\mathsf{Present}(\mathit{robot},Z_{\mathrm{pickup}}),\tau_1),\\
r_2 &= (\mathsf{DoorwayClear}(\mathit{locker}),\tau_2),\\
R(\mathit{locker},\mathsf{OPEN}) &= \{r_1,r_2\}.
\end{align}
The two requirements distinguish authenticated peer presence from an environmental condition.
The predicate in $r_1$ refers to the robot identified by the authenticated session, so detecting an arbitrary object in the pickup zone is insufficient.
The predicate in $r_2$ requires doorway clearance and can be evaluated independently of the robot's identity.

Each requirement has its own freshness bound because the physical conditions may change on different timescales.
A result may exceed its freshness bound while another required check is still being completed.
The locker therefore checks both results against their respective bounds immediately before opening.

\subsection{Verification Model}
\label{sec:verification-model}

A \emph{verification mechanism} obtains evidence about physical context and evaluates the predicate of a requirement.
A mechanism specifies the resources needed to obtain physical evidence and the rule for evaluating that evidence.
A local mechanism uses the action owner's sensing resources, while a cooperative mechanism requires participation from another endpoint.
In either case, the endpoint controlling the protected action is responsible for evaluating the evidence.

A mechanism is a candidate for a requirement only if it can verify the required predicate under the deployment's accepted assumptions.
For requirement $r_i$, we denote this candidate set by
\begin{equation}
M(r_i)=\{m\mid m\text{ can verify }p_i\}.
\end{equation}
Having the required hardware alone is insufficient to establish that a mechanism can verify the predicate.
For example, a mechanism that detects an unidentified object cannot independently satisfy a requirement for the presence of a named peer.

The authorization service constructs a \emph{verification plan} by selecting one executable candidate mechanism for each physical requirement of an action.
For the requirement set $R(d,a)$, the plan is
\begin{equation}
V(d,a)=\{(r_1,m_1^*),\ldots,(r_n,m_n^*)\},
\end{equation}
where $m_i^*\in M(r_i)$ is the mechanism selected for $r_i$.
The selected mechanisms may combine local and cooperative verification within the same action.
If a required predicate has no eligible, executable mechanism, the action cannot proceed.
The selection and provisioning procedure is described in Section~\ref{sec:selection}.

\figurename~\ref{fig:formulation-overview} illustrates these concepts using the robot--locker example.
Each endpoint controls its own action, which is subject to a set of physical requirements.
Each requirement specifies a physical condition and a freshness bound, and the verification plan assigns a local or cooperative mechanism to check that condition.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/formulation-overview.pdf}
    \caption{Conceptual relationships in the robot--locker example. Each endpoint's action has its own physical requirements, each consisting of a predicate and a freshness bound. A verification plan pairs each requirement with a selected mechanism.}
    \label{fig:formulation-overview}
\end{figure}

Verification succeeds at a decision time only when the evidence satisfies both the required predicate and its freshness bound.
Executing a selected mechanism obtains physical evidence and its local timestamp.
The endpoint evaluates the complete requirement at decision time $t$ through
\begin{equation}
\mathsf{Verify}(r_i,m_i^*,t)\in\{\mathsf{PASS},\mathsf{FAIL}\}.
\end{equation}
The result is $\mathsf{PASS}$ when the evidence meets the acceptance rule for $p_i$ under the mechanism's stated assumptions and satisfies $\tau_i$ at time $t$.
Missing, invalid, or expired evidence produces $\mathsf{FAIL}$.
A previous $\mathsf{PASS}$ does not remain valid automatically as the evidence ages.

An endpoint permits its action only when every physical requirement returns $\mathsf{PASS}$ at the action start time $t^a$.
Given valid operation authorization and a complete verification plan, this condition is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:allow}
\mathsf{Allow}(d,a) \iff \bigwedge\nolimits_{(r_i,m_i^*)\in V(d,a)} \bigl[\mathsf{Verify}(r_i,m_i^*,t^a)=\mathsf{PASS}\bigr].
\end{equation}
Sections~\ref{sec:execution} and~\ref{sec:freshness} describe how the endpoint enforces this condition.



\section{Verification Planning and Execution}
\label{sec:design}

In this section, we describe how the authorization service selects and provisions verification plans and handshake communication mechanisms, and how endpoints execute the plans and check freshness before acting.

\subsection{Verification Planning and Provisioning}
\label{sec:selection}

The authorization service constructs a verification plan by selecting an executable mechanism for each physical requirement of the requested action.
Algorithm~\ref{alg:verification-planning} summarizes the selection procedure.
The algorithm considers an operation in which a requester and a peer establish an authenticated session.
For each protected action, it retrieves $R(d,a)$ and considers the mechanisms in $M(r_i)$.
It determines the requester's available resources by intersecting its registered capabilities with the resources reported for the current operation.
For the peer, it uses the registered resources.
It matches each endpoint's resources against the requirements of its role in the candidate mechanism.
Local candidates require the action owner's sensing resources, while cooperative candidates require the resources needed for each participant's role.
Among the remaining mechanisms, it selects the highest-priority mechanism in the configured priority list.
If no mechanism remains for a required predicate, the request is rejected.

The provisioned plan identifies the action owner, action, requirements, selected mechanisms, participants, parameters, and freshness bounds.
Endpoints receive the plan from the authorization service over an authenticated channel and associate it with the requested operation.

The authorization service also determines which communication mechanism the endpoints use for their handshake.
It selects the highest-priority communication mechanism supported by both endpoints' available resources and provides this selection along with the verification plans.
The endpoints use the selected mechanism to exchange handshake messages and establish their authenticated session.


\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Verification Plan and Handshake Channel Selection}
\label{alg:verification-planning}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require Requested operation, requester $q$, peer $p$, and policy
\Require Mechanism and priority lists
\Require Registered resources $C_q$, $C_p$, and requester's reported resources $D_q$
\Ensure Verification plans $V(d,a)$ and a handshake channel $h$
\If{the operation fails conventional authorization}
    \State \Return rejection
\EndIf
\State $E_q \gets C_q \cap D_q$ \Comment{Available requester resources}
\State $E_p \gets C_p$ \Comment{Registered peer resources}
\For{each protected action $(d,a)$ in the operation}
    \State $V(d,a) \gets \emptyset$
    \For{each requirement $r_i \in R(d,a)$}
        \State Select the highest-priority $m_i^* \in M(r_i)$ whose role-specific resource requirements are met by $E_q$ and $E_p$
        \If{no such mechanism exists}
            \State \Return rejection
        \EndIf
        \State $V(d,a) \gets V(d,a) \cup \{(r_i,m_i^*)\}$
    \EndFor
\EndFor
\State Select the highest-priority channel $h$ feasible with $E_q$ and $E_p$
\If{no such channel exists}
    \State \Return rejection
\EndIf
\State \Return all plans $V(d,a)$ and handshake channel $h$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}




\subsection{Verification Execution and Local Authorization}
\label{sec:execution}

Each endpoint follows the provisioned verification plan to verify the physical context required for its own action.
For each requirement, it executes the selected mechanism using the parameters specified in the plan.
It records the resulting physical evidence and the corresponding observation timestamps.

The endpoint obtains physical evidence either through its own sensors or through an exchange with an authenticated peer.
For local verification, it directly observes the relevant condition, such as whether the doorway is clear.
For cooperative verification, the endpoints first perform their handshake using the communication mechanism selected by the authorization service.
After establishing the authenticated session, they perform the physical exchange required by the selected verification mechanism.
The exchange uses their shared cryptographic context to link the physical responses to the authenticated peer and session.
Section~\ref{sec:mechanisms} describes cooperative co-presence mechanisms as instances of this verification process.

The endpoint permits its action only when all of that action's physical requirements are satisfied.
It evaluates the collected evidence according to each selected mechanism's acceptance rule and checks freshness immediately before the action begins, as described in Section~\ref{sec:freshness}.
If any required verification fails or cannot be completed, the endpoint denies the action.
This decision is made locally and does not require another round trip to the authorization service.

\subsection{Verification Freshness}
\label{sec:freshness}

The endpoint enforces the authorization condition in Equation~\eqref{eq:allow} by evaluating all requirements immediately before actuation.
For each requirement $r_i=(p_i,\tau_i)$, let $t_i^v$ be the time of the physical observation used to verify $p_i$, and let $t^a$ be the action start time, both measured using the verifier's local clock.
The freshness condition $0\leq t^a-t_i^v\leq\tau_i$ is evaluated inside $\mathsf{Verify}(r_i,m_i^*,t^a)$ together with the evidence for $p_i$.
Freshness is measured from the time of the physical observation, rather than the completion of subsequent processing.

All verification results must satisfy their respective freshness bounds when the action begins.
A result may expire while another required check is still running.
If any result has expired, the endpoint cannot proceed with the action using the current results.

\section{Cooperative Co-Presence Verification}
\label{sec:mechanisms}

In this section, we present co-presence verification as a representative example of using physical context to check an action's physical requirements.
Authentication establishes the peer's identity, but does not establish that the authenticated peer is physically present where the interaction takes place.
Co-presence verification addresses this gap by checking whether that peer is within the verifier's policy-defined interaction region.
We examine IR, acoustic signaling, LiFi, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and UWB as sources of co-presence or proximity evidence, with each mechanism's suitability determined by the deployment's assumptions.
These mechanisms use inexpensive emitters and receivers or existing wireless radios.

\subsection{IR}
\label{sec:mechanism-ir}

Our IR mechanism combines an optical exchange with a mutual, timed challenge--response inspired by Hancke--Kuhn distance bounding~\cite{hancke2005rfid}.
It targets the presence of an authenticated peer within a configured interaction zone, subject to the deployment assumptions below.
Both endpoints require an IR transmitter and receiver and participate as verifier and prover in the same execution.
The exchange begins after mutual authentication and session establishment, independently of the channel used for the preceding handshake.

\paragraph{Preparation phase.}
Preparation associates the IR exchange with the authenticated session and a fresh nonce pair.
Let $A$ be the handshake initiator and $B$ its peer; this role assignment determines who sends the first IR challenge without removing either endpoint's verifier role.
Both endpoints obtain the same verification parameters through the authenticated authorization path: a round count $N$, a minimum success fraction $\alpha$, and a per-round response-time limit $\theta_{\mathrm{IR}}$.
Endpoint $A$ sends a MAC-protected \texttt{HK\_INIT} containing a message type, session key identifier, and fresh nonce $n_A$.
Endpoint $B$ checks the identifier and MAC, generates $n_B$, and returns \texttt{HK\_READY} containing its message type, $n_B$, and a MAC that also covers the locally retained $n_A$.
This authenticates the association between READY and the current INIT without retransmitting $n_A$.
The nonce pair distinguishes executions under the same session key; no separate execution identifier is transmitted.
Parameter consistency relies on the common session-associated plan: the IR control messages neither carry nor compare the parameters.

The endpoints derive response registers from the shared session MAC key and both nonces, using separate labels for each prover direction and challenge value.
Domain separation distinguishes this derivation from control-message authentication and separates the two prover directions.
For each prover $P\in\{A,B\}$, the derivation supplies two $N$-bit registers, $R^P_0$ and $R^P_1$.
The endpoints also generate independent, unpredictable challenge sequences $c^A_1,\ldots,c^A_N$ and $c^B_1,\ldots,c^B_N$.
All register derivation and challenge generation occur before the timed exchange.
After validating \texttt{HK\_READY} and completing its preparation, $A$ waits a short guard interval before sending the first challenge; $B$ listens immediately after sending \texttt{HK\_READY}.

\paragraph{Mutual bit exchange.}
\figurename~\ref{fig:ir-mutual-exchange} shows the alternating sequence.
Endpoint $A$ begins with $c^A_1$.
For each challenge $c^A_i$, $B$ returns $r^B_i=R^B_{c^A_i}[i]$ and then sends its own challenge $c^B_i$.
Endpoint $A$ answers with $r^A_i=R^A_{c^B_i}[i]$ and, except in the last round, appends its next challenge $c^A_{i+1}$.
The first transmission contains only a challenge and the last only a response.
Thus, the exchange carries $4N$ bits and yields $N$ locally measured challenge--response intervals at each endpoint.
The two-bit transmissions serialize a response bit followed by a challenge bit; they do not encode both bits in one optical symbol.
The response is sent without an intentional waiting interval, while receiver-recovery spacing before the next challenge is outside the measured response interval.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \begin{tabular}{@{}rcl@{}}
        $A\rightarrow B$ & : & $c^A_1$ \\
        $B\rightarrow A$ & : & $r^B_1,\ c^B_1$ \\
        $A\rightarrow B$ & : & $r^A_1,\ c^A_2$ \\
        $B\rightarrow A$ & : & $r^B_2,\ c^B_2$ \\
        & $\vdots$ & \\
        $B\rightarrow A$ & : & $r^B_N,\ c^B_N$ \\
        $A\rightarrow B$ & : & $r^A_N$
    \end{tabular}
    \caption{Mutual IR exchange after session-bound preparation. Each endpoint verifies $N$ responses to its own challenges. Intermediate transmissions carry a response followed by a new challenge.}
    \label{fig:ir-mutual-exchange}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Scope of the presence claim.}
The optical coverage must correspond to the authorized interaction zone under the deployment's assumptions about openings, reflections, receiver sensitivity, and attacker equipment.
The timing limit constrains on-demand relays only when their earliest correct responses exceed that limit at the defined measurement boundaries, accounting for any processing time the attacker can save.
An execution is rejected when too few rounds remain correct and timely; a single late round need not cause rejection when $\alpha<1$.
Guessing and advance-query attacks require separate analysis, as does the effect of the mutual scheduling and error tolerance on attack acceptance.
We do not transfer an unmodified Hancke--Kuhn security bound to this construction.
The intended relay experiment introduces at least $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ of additional measured delay, but this is an experimental condition rather than a universal lower bound on relay latency.
Microsecond-scale software timing does not establish a meter-scale optical distance bound, and optical reachability across an open doorway does not by itself establish membership in the same room.

\subsection{Acoustic}
\label{sec:mechanism-acoustic}

Our proposed acoustic mechanism combines a session-bound response with the propagation delay of sound to check whether an authenticated peer is within the policy-defined interaction region.
Following Keyed Echo~\cite{sastry2003secure}, it delivers a challenge over a fast communication channel and receives the response acoustically.
The challenge channel need not be the channel used for the preceding handshake; the exchange relies on the shared cryptographic context established by that handshake.
Both endpoints require a speaker and microphone so that each can verify the other.

\paragraph{Mutual challenge--response.}
The exchange links a fresh acoustic response to the authenticated peer and measures how long that response takes to arrive.
The verifier sends an unpredictable nonce, and the peer returns a keyed response bound to that nonce, the session, and the verification direction.
The verifier checks both the response's authenticity and the interval from challenge transmission to complete response reception.
It accepts the exchange only when the response is valid and arrives within the configured time limit.
The endpoints then reverse roles and repeat the exchange with a new nonce, making independent decisions from their own observations.

\paragraph{Relay resistance.}
Relay resistance comes from the acoustic path that an outside emitter must traverse to reach the verifier.
A relay may forward the challenge or a valid keyed response over a fast link, but if its final emitter remains outside the authorized region, the response must still travel acoustically from that emitter to the verifier.
The unpredictable challenge prevents a valid response from being prepared in advance, except by guessing, while the time limit can reject responses whose acoustic path is too long.
Thus, this mechanism does not rely on every relay introducing a fixed processing delay; it relies on a lower bound on the time required for an outside emitter's response to arrive.

\paragraph{Timing requirements.}
The time limit must account for communication and processing delays before it can support a presence claim for a particular region.
Allowing extra time for an honest endpoint also gives a faster attacker more time to deliver a response from farther away.
Keyed Echo addresses this tradeoff by reducing the region in which location claims can be accepted as the allowed delay increases.
Our adaptation likewise requires a timing bound that excludes responses from outside the policy-defined region, accounting for packet transmission, processing, and measurement uncertainty.
A deadline chosen only to accommodate normal exchanges does not establish this bound.

\paragraph{Scope of the presence claim.}
Our acoustic presence claim excludes relays that can generate the peer's response inside the authorized region with sufficiently low delay.
An internal proxy could receive a remote peer's valid response over a fast link and replay it through a nearby speaker without learning the peer's key.
Excluding secret-key sharing therefore does not exclude this attack, and mutual verification does not remove it.
The claim also requires an upper bound on acoustic propagation speed over relevant paths, including paths through materials that carry sound faster than air.
Under these assumptions, a validated time limit can support presence within the configured region; it does not establish membership in the same room unless that region lies within the room.

\subsection{LiFi}
\label{sec:mechanism-lifi}

We also use LiFi to verify co-presence through visible-light communication.
We choose this approach because visible-light links can be built with inexpensive LEDs, optical receivers, and simple circuitry, as demonstrated by Wang et al.~\cite{wang2015low}.
Each endpoint uses an LED to transmit signals and an optical receiver to detect its peer's signals.

Co-presence verification follows the mutual challenge--response procedure used for IR in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-ir}.
After session establishment, the endpoints exchange challenges and responses over the visible-light channel, using the shared cryptographic context and fresh nonces to bind the exchange to the authenticated session.
Each endpoint independently checks whether enough responses to its own challenges are correct and arrive within the configured time limit.
The timing settings account for the visible-light receiver's response characteristics rather than reuse the IR settings unchanged.

The LiFi presence claim depends on the deployment's optical coverage and assumptions about relay capabilities.
The deployment must account for alignment, ambient illumination, reflections, and openings through which light can reach outside that region.
As with IR, a relay can forward valid responses without learning the session key; the timing check rejects an exchange when too few responses arrive within the limit.
A sufficiently fast relay can therefore fall within the acceptance conditions; using visible light alone does not exclude it or prove that the authenticated peer is in the same room.

\subsection{Bluetooth}
\label{sec:mechanism-bluetooth}

Our Bluetooth mechanism uses the received signal strength indicator (RSSI) of a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) connection for lightweight proximity screening.
RSSI is readily available from BLE radios and has been used for ranging and localization without additional sensing hardware~\cite{giovanelli2018rssi,faragher2015location}.
Both endpoints require a BLE radio, and the check operates after they establish an authenticated session over the BLE connection.
The mechanism evaluates signal strength rather than calculating a physical distance or performing a timed distance-bounding exchange.

Each endpoint independently evaluates RSSI observations from the connection carrying its authenticated session.
The authorization plan specifies a minimum RSSI, a sample count, and an interval between readings.
Each endpoint obtains the configured number of controller-reported RSSI values for that connection and accepts its local check when their median is at least the provisioned threshold.
The endpoints then exchange their medians and verdicts through authenticated session messages, with the handshake initiator reporting first.
The peer's report is informational and does not replace or alter the local decision; a failed RSSI read or an incomplete report exchange aborts verification.
Using the session's active connection avoids treating an unrelated beacon's signal strength as evidence about the authenticated peer.

An RSSI threshold supports a spatial interpretation only under deployment assumptions that justify the relationship between signal strength and the required region.
Transmit power, antenna orientation, multipath propagation, and obstructions can change this relationship, so the threshold must be calibrated for the deployment~\cite{faragher2015location,giovanelli2018rssi}.
An attacker can also amplify or relay valid Bluetooth signals while preserving session authentication, as demonstrated by Staat et al.~\cite{staat2022analog}.
Consequently, a passing RSSI check establishes sufficiently strong received signals on the measured link, but does not by itself establish relay-resistant peer presence, a secure distance upper bound, or membership in the same room.
A policy requiring such assurance must use a mechanism with adequate evidence under its accepted assumptions; RSSI alone is insufficient when amplification or relaying remains possible.

\subsection{Wi-Fi}
\label{sec:mechanism-wifi}

Our Wi-Fi mechanism uses RSSI for proximity screening over a direct endpoint-to-endpoint link.
The C implementation reads RSSI through the Linux \texttt{iw} utility, aggregates readings by their median, and compares a log-distance path-loss estimate with a configured distance threshold.
The endpoints alternate access-point and station roles so that each evaluates its own RSSI observations as the station.

Verification follows the local-decision structure of Bluetooth in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-bluetooth}, with measurements associated with the authenticated peer's direct link and evaluated under provisioned sampling and threshold parameters.
Observing a shared infrastructure access point alone does not measure the distance between the two endpoints.
As with Bluetooth, RSSI requires deployment calibration and remains sensitive to transmit power, multipath, and obstructions~\cite{bahl2000radar,kotaru2015spotfi}; a passing check does not by itself establish relay-resistant presence or a secure distance upper bound.

\subsection{UWB}
\label{sec:mechanism-uwb}

Our UWB mechanism uses time-of-flight ranging to check quantitative proximity requirements.
The endpoints establish their authenticated SST session over TCP; UWB is used for ranging, while coordination and result reports remain on the secure TCP connection.

Each endpoint independently evaluates distances obtained by initiating a double-sided two-way ranging (DS-TWR) exchange.
The requester measures first, and the endpoints then reverse roles so that the target obtains its own measurements.
The authorization plan specifies the required sample count, collection deadline, and maximum distance.
A local check passes only when the required number of successful measurements is collected within the deadline and their median does not exceed the distance threshold; the peer's reported result is informational.
Direction-specific ranging configuration is derived from the session MAC key to associate the radio configuration with the authenticated session.

The current static-STS configuration is reused across executions under the same session key and does not provide per-execution waveform freshness.
A passing check provides proximity evidence under the deployment's calibration and propagation assumptions; claiming a secure distance upper bound additionally requires validating the ranging waveform and receiver.
Interpreting that distance as membership in a pickup zone or room also requires a justified mapping between the threshold and the authorized region.

% An authenticated application packet accompanying an unrelated range measurement is insufficient to establish that binding.
% The ranging protocol and hardware must connect the timed exchange to the credentialed participant.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:implementation}

\subsection{SST Integration}
\label{sec:implementation-overview}

We implement our prototype by extending the Secure Swarm Toolkit (SST)~\cite{kim2017toolkit} with verification planning and physical-channel verification.
SST's Java-based authorization service, \emph{Auth}~\cite{kim2016secure}, provides entity registration, conventional authorization, and session-key distribution.
The robot and locker applications use the SST C API~\cite{kim2023sst} on Raspberry Pi endpoints.
Auth provides both the policy decision point for operation requests and the key distribution center for peer sessions; the architecture does not require these functions to reside in the same service.

We extend Auth's registration and policy data to describe the resources and checks needed for physical verification.
Entity records identify sensors and actuators, action policies list required checks, and an ordered mechanism catalog specifies resource requirements and execution parameters.
Requests can report currently available resources and name a specific target endpoint at runtime.
Auth uses these data to select feasible verification methods and a separate handshake transport, following Section~\ref{sec:selection}.
A request is rejected before key issuance if a required method or handshake transport cannot be selected.
The implemented selection checks resource availability; the deployment assumptions that make a mechanism suitable for a spatial predicate must be established separately.

Auth provisions the verification plan through the existing authenticated session-key distribution path.
The plan is serialized as JSON in the session's cryptographic specification and retained with the session key at each endpoint.
It identifies the requester and targets, required checks, verification topology, selected methods and parameters, and handshake transport.
For TCP, Auth also supplies the selected target's network address.
This associates the physical verification configuration with the session without requiring Auth to participate in the subsequent physical exchange.

\subsection{Endpoint Verification Runtime}
\label{sec:implementation-runtime}

Both endpoints execute the selected co-presence mechanism after establishing an authenticated peer session.
The applications read the session-associated plan and dispatch the \texttt{CO\_LOCATION} check to IR, LiFi, acoustic, BLE RSSI, or UWB verification.
Each endpoint evaluates its own measurements and stops the application flow if its check fails or the exchange aborts.
Malformed plans, invalid mechanism parameters, and selected mechanisms unavailable in the build are rejected.
The mechanisms also check session-key expiration before execution and before returning a successful result.

The prototype supports TCP, IR, LiFi, and acoustic signaling as transports for SST's three-message peer handshake.
The applications select this transport through a runtime option, while the provisioned plan selects the subsequent co-presence mechanism independently.
Endpoint communication with Auth uses TCP regardless of the peer-handshake transport.
IR and LiFi verification can follow any supported handshake transport; the current acoustic Keyed Echo implementation requires the authenticated TCP socket for its control messages.
The physical handshake adapters establish the session's cryptographic context but do not yet provide ongoing secure application messaging over those channels.

The implemented endpoint path covers cooperative verification and application-level rejection, while complete actuation enforcement remains to be integrated.
The examples do not operate a physical door or gripper, enforce independent plans for every endpoint action, or implement the observation-to-action freshness gate of Section~\ref{sec:freshness}.
Session-key expiration and mechanism response deadlines are enforced, but neither substitutes for an action's freshness bound.

\subsection{Hardware and Sensing Implementation}
\label{sec:implementation-mechanisms}

Each physical endpoint runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B with the sensing and communication components described below.

\noindent
\textbf{IR.}
Each endpoint uses a transmitter and a demodulating receiver from a DORHEA $38\,\mathrm{kHz}$ IR module kit, connected to Raspberry Pi GPIO pins.
The pigpio library generates approximately $38\,\mathrm{kHz}$ carrier bursts, with nominal $300$ and $600\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ durations for the two bit values.
Framed byte messages carry the handshake and verification preparation, while the timed exchange sends individual bits directly.
OpenSSL supplies random challenges and nonces, HMAC-SHA-256 authentication, and response-register derivation for the protocol in Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-ir}.
Each response interval is measured from the observed completion of challenge transmission to the end of the received response pulse used for decoding.
The implementation supports $32$, $64$, or $128$ rounds and applies the plan's success fraction and per-response deadline independently at each endpoint.
It inserts a $50\,\mathrm{ms}$ recovery interval between a response and the next challenge, outside the measured response interval.

\noindent
\textbf{Acoustic.}
Each endpoint uses a commodity USB speaker and USB microphone connected to the Raspberry Pi.
ALSA and ggwave handle audio at $48\,\mathrm{kHz}$ mono, 16-bit PCM, with signaling starting near $10.5\,\mathrm{kHz}$ to accommodate the devices' frequency response; this configuration includes audible frequencies.
Each acoustic response carries a $16$-byte HMAC-SHA-256 tag computed using the session MAC key over a fresh $16$-byte TCP challenge nonce and the verification direction.
The verifier uses \texttt{CLOCK\_MONOTONIC} to measure the interval from secure challenge transmission to completed acoustic decoding, including network, audio, and software delays.

\noindent
\textbf{LiFi.}
Each endpoint uses a small red LED with a simple GPIO-controlled drive circuit and a TEMT6000 phototransistor receiver.
The implementation applies the mutual verification procedure of Section~\ref{sec:mechanism-lifi} using pigpio-generated dark intervals of $600$ or $1200\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and a $900\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ received-width threshold.
GPIO assignments and LED polarity are configurable for each endpoint.
LiFi uses its own response-register derivation labels and physical-layer settings, including a $50\,\mathrm{ms}$ recovery interval between a response and the next challenge outside the measured interval.

\noindent
\textbf{Bluetooth.}
Each endpoint uses the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B's onboard BLE radio.
The C implementation uses Linux BlueZ interfaces to establish a BLE L2CAP connection and carry SST's peer handshake and secure messages over that connection.
It obtains the connection's HCI handle and reads RSSI directly through BlueZ's \texttt{hci\_read\_rssi} API.
The verification plan supplies the sample count, interval, and minimum RSSI; each endpoint compares its median RSSI with the threshold.
The endpoints exchange their medians and verdicts through secure session messages, with the handshake initiator reporting first; each endpoint retains its own measurement as the basis of its decision.

\noindent
\textbf{Wi-Fi.}
Each endpoint uses a TP-Link Archer T2U Nano AC600 USB Wi-Fi adapter connected to its Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.
The adapter provides a dedicated measurement link while the onboard Wi-Fi remains available for remote access.
One endpoint operates as an access point and the other associates with it as a station.
The station sends probe traffic over the direct link and reads the driver-reported RSSI through the Linux \texttt{iw} utility after receiving each response.
The endpoints then swap roles and repeat the procedure so that both obtain their own observations.
The C implementation aggregates samples by their median, converts the median to a distance estimate using configurable reference RSSI and path-loss parameters, and compares that estimate with the configured distance threshold.
The access point logs the station's reported result; each endpoint judges proximity from its own station-side measurements.
Amplification or relaying can satisfy the RSSI threshold while the peer remains distant, so this implementation does not by itself provide relay-resistant presence verification.

\noindent
\textbf{UWB.}
Each endpoint uses a Qorvo DWM3001CDK board connected to its Raspberry Pi through the board's J20 USB interface.
The C driver communicates directly with the USB serial device running Qorvo's DW3\_QM33\_SDK CLI firmware and controls FiRa DS-TWR using \texttt{INITF} and \texttt{RESPF} commands.
The board performs the radio timing, and the Raspberry Pi collects successful distance reports in centimeters.
HMAC-SHA-256 with the SST session MAC key and a direction-specific label derives the FiRa session identifier and eight-byte static-STS \texttt{vupper64} value.
The endpoints coordinate both ranging directions over the TCP SST session and evaluate their own distance medians against the provisioned threshold.
